purpose: A local seasonal starting point for outdoor HydroPip tower crop selection. It uses the saved USDA zone and current month without requiring a live weather lookup.
limitations: USDA hardiness zones describe average annual extreme minimum temperatures, not complete vegetable planting dates.
Saved location, exposure, elevation, and the grower's observed microclimate should refine this calendar when available.
Live weather is an exception check for unusual heat, frost, storms, or a crop near its tolerance limit, not a default requirement.

sources.name: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map - How to Use the Maps
sources.note: Explains that zones use 30-year average annual extreme minimum temperatures and that microclimates still matter.

sources.name: Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
sources.note: Provides region-specific outdoor vegetable planting windows for North, Central, and South Florida.

sources.name: UGA Vegetable Gardening in Georgia
sources.note: Provides spring and fall crop windows and succession-planting guidance for a warm southeastern climate.

sources.name: University of Minnesota Planting the Vegetable Garden
sources.note: Provides cool-season, warm-season, and fall succession timing for a short northern growing season.

sources.name: University of Arizona Maricopa County Vegetable Planting Calendar
sources.note: Shows why hot low-desert locations need different seasonal windows even when hardiness zones overlap humid regions.

indoor_protected.label: protected and planning season
indoor_protected.summary: Use protected starts or an indoor growing area while preparing the next outdoor tower cycle.
systemNotes: Protect exposed feed tubing and plants from freezing.
Use this period to clean, reset, and stage media for the next tower turn.

cool_prime.label: cool-season tower window
cool_prime.summary: This is the strongest window for compact leafy greens, brassica greens, and cool-season herbs.
avoidNow: overloading towers with long-season fruiting crops
systemNotes: Use succession batches every 2-3 weeks for steadier harvests.
Cooler conditions usually require fewer or shorter feed windows than summer.

warm_transition.label: warm-season transition
warm_transition.summary: Keep quick greens producing while adding heat-tolerant herbs and compact warm-season crops.
avoidNow: large vining crops without separate support
crowding fruiting crops into every pocket
systemNotes: Reserve most pockets for greens and herbs; fruiting crops need support and closer nutrient monitoring.
Recalibrate feed timing as days warm.

warm_prime.label: warm-season tower window
warm_prime.summary: Favor heat-tolerant herbs, resilient greens, and a limited number of supported fruiting plants.
startNext: fall greens near the end of the window
avoidNow: cool-season lettuce in full afternoon sun
systemNotes: Use shade during the harshest afternoon exposure when needed.
Watch media moisture and tune short feed windows by runoff.

summer_heat.label: peak-heat tower window
summer_heat.summary: Keep the towers productive with crops that tolerate heat, then stage cool-season seedlings for the next break in temperature.
startNext: leaf lettuce in a cooler nursery area
avoidNow: standard head lettuce in full sun
adding nutrients before checking pH and EC
systemNotes: Use afternoon shade where exposure is harsh.
Increase feed frequency only after checking media moisture and runoff; do not simply lengthen every cycle.

fall_transition.label: cool-season reset window
fall_transition.summary: Finish productive warm crops while starting the next high-output cycle of greens and herbs.
avoidNow: starting too many long-season fruiting plants
waiting until every mature plant stops producing before resetting
systemNotes: Move healthy mature plants to raised beds when appropriate, recover the media, and turn tower pockets quickly.
Reduce summer feed frequency as temperatures and day length fall.
